summary:
I had a lot of fun chatting with Rob about METR's work. I stand by my claims here that the world is not on track to keep risk from AI to an acceptable level, and we desperately need more people working on these problems.
Quoting @robertwiblin
AI models currently have a 50% chance of doing something that takes a human expert one hour.
This doubles every 7 months.
In 2 years? They could automate full workdays. In 4 years? A full month.
I discuss the most important graph in AI today with Beth Barnes, the CEO of METR, which uncovered this rule of AI progress.
Her bottom line: "It really doesn't seem like 2 years would be surprising for recursively self-improving AI."
Beth also explains: where company safety testing fails, why there are no true closed-weight models, AI undermines leading powers, why she's come around on open weighting, and why models might be about to start playing dumb much more often.

linked_urls.title: Measuring AI Ability to Complete Long Tasks - METR
linked_urls.summary: We propose measuring AI performance in terms of the *length* of tasks AI agents can complete. We show that this metric has been consistently exponentially increasing over the past 6 years, with a doubling time of around 7 months. Extrapolating this trend predicts that, in under a decade, we will see AI agents that can independently complete a large fraction of software tasks that currently take humans days or weeks.

title: METR (@METR_Evals)
summary:
One reason I like making tasks that are much harder than what the current best AIs can complete is that it acts as a sort of preregistration about the distribution of tasks we think AIs should be able to do in the future.
You could imagine when a new model comes out creating a bunch of tasks then, and then running previous models on them to compare. But you're likely to be biased in the tasks you create based on other information you have about AI progress (i.e. what kinds of tasks you already know new models can complete), which might cause you to overestimate progress (look, this new model can do these crazy hard tasks we just came up with!).
But preregistering forces your hand (hmm okay it can do some crazy things, but it also can't do these reasonable things we thought it might be able to do by now).
Conversely if the model really can do most of the preregistered tasks, you know that's a more meaningful capability boost and isn't (necessarily) as heavily selected/cherry-picked.

title: METR (@METR_Evals)
summary:
Widespread use of AI agents creates a unique opportunity to understand and quantify previously illegible work processes, for two reasons:
- AI agent transcripts provide much more detailed logs of how some work was done than any human worker would ~ever produce, at a massive scale
- cheap AI agent labor allow us to scalably analyze billions of tokens of such logs and extract quantitative and qualitative insights
I think this is a very promising direction for studying the impacts and evolution of AI R&D automation (and creating transparency around the activities at frontier AI developers in general). I'm very excited about this exploratory work by my colleague Amy demonstrating one application of this - upper bounding the productivity impact of AI agents.
For now I think this very simple bound is surprisingly non-trivial: after adjusting for the limited portion of their day engineers spend using AI agents, this indicates to me that the median METR engineer is not getting >2x uplift from AI agents (my guess is it's significantly lower). But this particular bound will likely become a significant overestimate of productivity impacts in the near future, as Amy discusses in the post.
But this is only scratching the surface of what we could get from analyzing transcripts with more sophisticated methods in the future!

title: METR (@METR_Evals)
summary:
While recent developments have surprised me and our current evidence base has many limitations, I would still bet that, if we have an otherwise similar distribution of harder evals capable of measuring this, we'll find 50% time horizons to be below 100h by EOY. I think dramatic (e.g. 2x increase in pace of overall progress) AI R&D acceleration is indeed hard to rule out but <10% likely.
Why? I suspect (but can't be sure!) that current numbers are mildly inflated by saturation, and in particular I don't think the upper CIs are very credible (though this is based on other evidence, the time horizon 1.1 benchmark indeed cannot provide decisive evidence against high time horizons anymore). Seeing >3 doublings over the rest of this year to get above 100h seems plausible but is meaningfully above my median guess.
Separately, I think agents might be increasingly overfit to the kinds of tasks that are in our suite, making it less predictive about broader impacts than it has been in the past. We're trying to develop more nuanced methodologies for assessing this, but I think it's plausible that models will eventually reach time horizons of >100 hours on our historical task distributions while having effective time horizons many times shorter for many critical messy real world tasks.
A key open question for me this year is what happens if models do reach ~superhuman performance on a large class of well-specified software tasks, while remaining limited on messier or more open ended ones. I could imagine this being very transformative, but non-SWE bottlenecks could prevent it from speeding up further AI R&D progress significantly.
Overall, current evidence is indeed unclear and we should be prepared for the possibility of things speeding up further, but it's not my central guess. I think there's a ton of low hanging fruit that could greatly inform us about this that the world could collect over the coming months. The mood at METR right now is one of intense debate and urgency and aliveness, we are figuring this out in real time (though we've been here before and then developed new methodologies that gave us renewed clarity!)

title: METR (@METR_Evals)
clean_title: Monitoring AI agents with automated LLM systems as tasks become more abstract
summary:
To evaluate our monitoring systems, we typically rely on a pretty strong assumption that we've given agents a concrete, narrowly scoped task. But we're going to give agents increasingly abstract/high-level tasks as they get better.
This means (to the extent they’re misaligned) they’ll be able to justify a bunch of pretty unrelated stuff as being part of their assigned goal. I think this might be an important way that our monitorability trends don't capture the actual dynamics here, since we typically evaluate on a fixed distribution of tasks.
Quoting @idavidrein
Frontier AI labs like OpenAI and Anthropic have started using automated LLM monitoring systems to make sure their internal AI agents stay aligned [1, 2]. I think this is really important and good! Unfortunately, it's difficult to get perfect coverage with these systems, and there are many ways the systems can be subverted (like ~all software).
AI companies doing large-scale internal deployments of agents with lots of resources/affordances (e.g. agents can spin up compute environments themselves, have broad permissions or inherit authentication from their human operator) should (a) have a basic LLM-based monitoring system for their agents, and (b) should maintain a clear list of all of the known gaps and vulnerabilities of this system.
[1]
[2] (section 5.5, especially 5.5.1.1)
clean_summary: Evaluating monitoring systems often assumes agents are given concrete, narrowly scoped tasks. However, as agents handle more abstract or high-level tasks, they may justify unrelated actions as part of their goals, which can challenge monitorability assessments. Frontier AI labs like OpenAI and Anthropic are using automated LLM monitoring to keep AI agents aligned, but these systems are not perfect and can be subverted, similar to software vulnerabilities. AI companies deploying large-scale agents with broad permissions should implement basic LLM-based monitoring and maintain a clear list of known gaps and vulnerabilities in these systems.
